articles.title: Building Safer Medication Safety AI: Association Is Not Causation
articles.description: Medication-related AI can help detect potential adverse drug reactions by analysing medication histories, clinical notes, laboratory results, symptoms, and treatment timelines. However, a major technical challenge remains: distinguishing a genuine medication-related event from a coincidental clinical occurrence. Consider a patient who develops nausea after starting a new medication. A machine learning model may identify a strong association between the drug and the symptom. Yet the patient could have an underlying gastrointestinal condition, an infection, or another medication contributing to the event. A robust medication safety pipeline should therefore go beyond simple co-occurrence detection. It should establish medication exposure and timing, examine dosage and possible interactions, incorporate relevant patient characteristics, identify competing explanations, and communicate the confidence and limitations of its findings. This also requires careful handling of observational data. Confounding by indication, reporting bias, incomplete medication histories, and inconsistent clinical documentation can all distort the relationship between a drug and an observed outcome. AI can support pharmacovigilance through signal detection, case prioritisation, pattern discovery, and explainable risk assessment. However, a detected signal should remain a signal until appropriately investigated. For agentic AI, the architecture needs an additional safety layer. Detecting a suspected adverse event should not automatically authorise treatment modification. Systems need clearly defined permissions, escalation pathways, human approval where appropriate, and auditable records of their recommendations and actions. The engineering objective should be to build systems that recognise possible harm while remaining honest about what the evidence can establish. If you are developing medication safety, pharmacovigilance, or healthcare AI systems, prioritise causality-aware reasoning and clinically governed escalation in your design.

articles.title: Ten engines for one box: which local inference engine fits a 100 GB rig with two 16 GB cards?
articles.description: This blog has published notes on ten inference engines — llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM, Sonar (formerly Aphrodite Engine), exo, ExLlamaV3 + TabbyAPI, Strata, PolyStrata, Avalon and Xolotl. This is the decision piece: which of them I would run on the machine I keep being asked about — roughly 100 GB of system RAM and two 16 GB consumer GPUs. Every figure below I have checked; none is estimated or invented. All are published numbers collected on our benchmark page, https://localai.hex7.com/benchmark.html, which marks every one with a source and dashes where none was found. Self-reported figures are labelled as such, third-party measurements likewise, and where no comparison can be made I say so — that is part of the conclusion, not a hedge. The engines, and what each one descends from Five of these projects descend from one another; the lineage matters before any comparison. llama.cpp (ggml-org): the general runtime on ggml — GGUF weights, an OpenAI-compatible server (llama serve), offload flags like --n-gpu-layers. Strata's and PolyStrata's head-to-heads benchmark against it first. Ollama: wraps that engine — inventivehq describes "the same weights through the Ollama wrapper" — with an MTP draft enabled by default. vLLM: contributes the high-concurrency design Sonar inherits: continuous batching, paged KV-cache management. Sonar (formerly Aphrodite Engine) is not a successor but the same repository renamed in place: commit "feat!: rename Aphrodite Engine to Sonar", 7 November 2026; PygmalionAI/aphrodite-engine redirects to dphnAI/sonar. Its README: "Sonar is based on vLLM." exo (exo-explore): a peer-to-peer cluster runtime on MLX — one model across several machines rather than inside one. ExLlamaV3 + TabbyAPI: the pair as it ships today. ExLlamaV3 is MIT-licensed, at v1.6.6 (31 Oct 2026); TabbyAPI is the OpenAI-compatible server that fronts it and has carried only its back-end since 14 July 2026. Strata (Niko1221): uses llama.cpp's raw materials — GGUF files, quantisation formats, the ggml kernel lineage — but is an overfit engine built on those formats, not a branch of its source. PolyStrata (simplexai-labs): a fork of Strata running two engines: keeps "the Strata project's, unchanged" for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, adds its own backends for roughly eleven more models. Avalon (freriadoc): a fork of llama.cpp (base merged to 31 October 2026) tuned for one model whose experts live in system RAM it owns. Xolotl (Indras-Mirror): a descendant of Strata — its README says "Built from Strata"; the parent's engine merged at 0.1.44.1, over 70,000 lines added on top. The capabilities table Before any speed number: what each engine can hold, and where it may put it. Engine Weights it reads Weights in system RAM? API surface Licence Purpose llama.cpp GGUF (k-/i-quants, MXFP4) Yes — but OS-paged: layer offload, -cpu-moe OpenAI-compatible server + UI MIT General runtime; thousands of models, every backend Ollama GGUF through llama.cpp Same levers, via the wrapper Its own API; OpenAI-style endpoint Appliance: installs with one command vLLM HF safetensors; GPTQ/INT4/FP8 as tested No — weights on GPUs; KV paged in VRAM Its own server Apache-2.0 Throughput for many concurrent users Sonar (ex-Aphrodite) HF-compatible, added formats incl. exl3 None documented; takes 92% of card VRAM "by design" OpenAI, Anthropic, Kobold, etc. AGPL-3.0 vLLM-line serving, added formats, roleplay samplers exo HF safetensors through MLX No — split across machines, not tiers in one OpenAI Chat/Responses, Claude Messages, Ollama One model across a machine cluster ExLlamaV3 + TabbyAPI EXL3 (QTIP) weights on the card; CPU offload documented for MoE experts only OpenAI-compatible FastAPI (TabbyAPI) MIT (ExLlamaV3) / AGPL-3.0 (TabbyAPI) VRAM-resident generation on one or two cards Strata GGUF quant formats (IQ-, GSQ-family) Partly — per-expert VRAM cache; rest read from SSD, not OS paging OpenAI + Anthropic-compatible Desktop appliance for a short list of model families PolyStrata Strata's engine, plus its own models Yes — knobs: --ram-experts-mib, hot-expert budget, --lock-experts Local servers per model; MCP server Many large MoEs on an ordinary PC Avalon Custom IQ3_K/IQ3_KS hybrids stock llama.cpp cannot load Yes — experts in its own pinned O_DIRECT RAM arena, LRU-managed OpenAI-compatible on :8080 One model pushed far on deliberately old hardware Xolotl GSQ-family and XQ weights, mixed precision Yes — three tiers: VRAM, pinned RAM arena by DMA, NVMe One OpenAI + Anthropic endpoint Huge MoEs on one box via heavy RAM + NVMe tiering The third column is where this hardware decides: whether an engine owns its weight placement or trusts somebody else's page cache. Sonar and TabbyAPI's AGPL-3.0 also rules them out of stacks that cannot ship AGPL; eight of these licences were checked against LICENSE files in my source notes, and the three general-runtime ones are as their repositories state. The machine at issue — and what cannot be compared My rig: about 100 GB of system RAM with two 16 GB consumer GPUs. Up front, honestly: no published benchmark row exists for this exact machine. What exists are runs on boxes adjacent to mine; an argument has to be built from those, and I read them against my budget below. All sources are listed at the end. What runs on a 2× 16 GB + 100 GB rig — the closest published runs Published run — machine as published Model / weights What was published RTX 4090 + 5700X + 110 GB DDR4 + NVMe, Linux DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (552B params) at V4 XQ weights 32.6 tok/s decode inside agent tasks; 41.1 in fast mode; prefill 258–439 — Xolotl README (self-reported) RTX 5090 D v2, 128 GB (community run) same family, UD-Q4_XS (136.7 GB) 8.6–10.6 tok/s — PolyStrata community file 2 × RTX 4090, EPYC 7443 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Q4_0 (93.7 GiB) 34.78 → 64.39 tok/s with -cmoe --moe-cache-mib 15000, prompt 440.7 → 321.5 — write-up of llama.cpp PRs #29887/#30112 2 × TITAN RTX, 125 GiB RAM (community run) Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_S decode 70.9–77.3, prompt 868.9–1,626.9 at 4K–128K — Strata community file 2 × RTX A4000 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, two-stage pipeline prefill of a 19K prompt: 1,079–1,190 → 1,669–1,761 with its pipeline — README (self-reported); untested beyond two GPUs RTX 4070 Laptop 8 GB, 32 GB — smallest card tested Qwen3.6-35B-A3B UD-Q3_K_M (17.1 GB), same file both engines PolyStrata vs llama.cpp b11540 94–100 write / 1,690 read vs 44.4 (41.5 at 32K) MTP-tuned llama.cpp, prompt 483–494 — PolyStrata's own head-to-head (self-reported) RTX 3060 12 GB + 64 GB; and a 5070 with 64 GB (community runs) Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Q2_0 / DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash prefill 882–981, decode 39–45 on the 3060; DeepSeek: prefill 121–231, decode 4.7 on the 5070 — Xolotl's WILL_IT_RUN.md RX 7900 XTX + R9700 (two cards), 96 GB DDR4 Ornith 1.5 122B Q5_K_M (82.6 GiB), same file, 128K context PolyStrata vs llama.cpp (Vulkan) a 98K prompt read in 184 s instead of 527 — 2.9×; llama.cpp wrote 13.5 tok/s at 100K — PolyStrata community file Read these rows against my budget, not against each other. Closest to mine: Strata's 2 × TITAN RTX community run — a generation above my cards, but a consumer two-card layout with expert caching that works; Avalon's A4000 pair is the only two-card pipeline test published at professional-card scale, though its result is prompt reading, not decode; Xolotl's measured machine is my RAM class plus one card — its README states an 80 GB expert arena on a 110 GB machine, 64 GB on a 90 GB one, so my rig sits between two documented cases, not outside them; PolyStrata goes down to an 8 GB laptop card and advertises multi-GPU on two or three cards, though honestly its largest model (GLM 5.3 Flash, 79–114 GB) "needs a 32 GB card to run at all" — on my box that means the class it demonstrated at laptop scale. The argument for PolyStrata and Xolotl on this box The case is not "these engines are faster" as a universal claim — no published head-to-head of PolyStrata against Xolotl exists on any machine, so that comparison cannot be made. The case is narrower: on exactly this budget — one box, two consumer cards, ~100 GB RAM — the published runs and documented memory designs are the ones that fit. The fix is what separates them on my hardware; three projects discovered the same problem independently. Avalon's README states it: the OS page cache is shared, so any other program pushes experts out mid-token; and the driver limits registered GPU memory to RAM − RAM/64 − 1.5 GiB, so a long prompt on a small machine ends in a crash. Its fix — a pre-registered, LRU-managed O_DIRECT arena inside the engine's own RAM — turns that crash into ~49 tok/s on 16 GB, where the page-cache path reached 13–17 and then crashed. Xolotl states the same tiering as an explicit budget: hot experts in VRAM, tens of gigabytes pinned in RAM read by DMA, the rest on NVMe moved a router layer ahead. PolyStrata landed in the same place: since 0.1.45-poly.7 it stopped holding file parts already on the card (Qwen3.6 after a 32K prompt: 17.9 GiB held → 13.1 GiB, same speed), and its knobs carry numbers — hold 6,144 MiB instead of everything and peak during a 32K prompt drops from 14.0 to 7.3 GiB for a 3–14% write cost; budget the hot-expert set to free RAM minus 4 GiB and first-chat decode rises from 51 to 57–60, after a 24K prompt from 75–78 to 77–85. The lesson all three teach: an engine must own its memory, or the machine takes it back mid-token. The table above shows this pattern landing on boxes like mine — Strata's two-card row, Xolotl's Gauntlet rows, PolyStrata at laptop scale, the two-AMD-cards prompt test. Where unowned paging falls out is just as published: the tuned llama.cpp row reaches 64.39 but loses prompt speed doing it, and its community row at 8.6–10.6 tok/s shows what a 136.7 GB file costs at my model class. The starkest pair on the benchmark page is Strata's head-to-head on a 12 GB RTX 3060 with 46 GB RAM: llama.cpp tuned with -ngl 99 -ncmoe manages 9.1–9.8 decode and 294–338 prompt; Strata, in the same run on the same file, publishes 41.6–41.9 and 910–1,050 — published by the Strata team, though it names llama.cpp's numbers. So for this machine I would run PolyStrata (its knobs match my RAM budget, its multi-card support exists, and its smallest published runs need less than I have) or Xolotl (measured on my RAM class with one card more; its tiering documentation states my RAM case). Both descend from Strata — PolyStrata is a fork of it running two engines; Xolotl says "Built from Strata" — and their caveats are honest: Xolotl is research code from one developer, Linux-first (its Windows path exists only for the DeepSeek model); PolyStrata marks its own extra backends experimental. Neither claim is universal; on other hardware the answer flips. Where the other engines are the right answer instead High-concurrency serving on data-centre cards: vLLM and Sonar If the box has H-class memory and many concurrent users, these are the answer. The measured H100 row (by the hosting company) puts vLLM at 120 tok/s at one request, 650 at ten, 1,850 at fifty, 2,400 at one hundred, first token 380 ms at fifty; on eight GB200 vLLM reports 26.2K prefill and 10.1K decode TPGS (their metric: tokens per GPU per second), and 7,360 tokens/GPU/s single-GPU prefill on a GB300/B300. Sonar's tuned four-RTX-PRO-6000 run (self-reported) reaches aggregate decode 428.3 → 1,083.3 tok/s at C=8 with DSpark speculation over a 2,674-token prompt — and the only published Sonar-vs-vLLM row on an H100 is modelled estimates by the publisher (48 / 380 / 1,450), not measurements of Sonar. On two consumer cards its docs advise care: no NVLink domain, 92% of the card "by design"; nothing in its pages tiers weights into system RAM, so my 100 GB buys Sonar nothing. An OpenAI-compatible box that works out of the installation command: Ollama The simplest case — one command installed, clients pointed at an OpenAI-style endpoint — is what Ollama is for; it inherits llama.cpp's offload levers. The rows show where it stands under the wrapper: same weights on a rented 5090, llama.cpp generated 249 tok/s with 83 ms to first token, Ollama 108 with 221 ms; on older desktop and M3 Max rows llama.cpp led again, 77.0 vs 69.1 and 53.5 vs 46.2. The one case it beats bare llama.cpp is its default MTP draft: 39.9 → 76.2 (L40S: 57.3; RTX 5090: 129.7). Use it when the wrapper, not the benchmark, is what you need. VRAM-resident EXL3 weights for single-card fast generation: ExLlamaV3 + TabbyAPI The project's earlier weights format has a run table published by its own maintainers (measured only against their first release — there is no comparison with other engines) and those numbers are the fastest thing on record for this family: 211 tok/s on Llama-2-7B at 4.0 bpw, 50 on CodeLlama-34B at 4.0 bpw, 38 on Llama-2-70B at 2.5 bpw, on the named 3090 Ti and 4090. ExLlamaV3 publishes no equivalent table, so its speed case rests on those earlier measurements; what V3 does document is CPU offloading for MoE experts, which changes what a two-card box can hold. For one card where the weights fit, hard to beat — but no EXL3-versus-GGUF comparison is published anywhere I could find. A cluster of separate machines rather than one box: exo If the memory ceiling need not be one machine's, exo is the answer: four M3 Ultra Mac Studios with 1.5 TB combined, measured by a journalist (Geerling), ran Qwen3-235B at about 32 tok/s and Kimi K2 Thinking around 30, with RDMA cutting memory-access latency from ~300 µs to under 50 — while llama.cpp's RPC layer-spreading got slower as nodes were added (no number published). On my rig exo is not a deployment today: Linux is CPU-only, and Mac nodes refuse to join Linux nodes. The general runtime, and the older siblings llama.cpp stays right when "whichever model shipped this week" matters, or when tuned flags make a big MoE run at all — 64.39 tok/s with -cmoe on two 4090s is llama.cpp. Strata and Avalon remain right for single-card desktops, but scope themselves to one model family; PolyStrata and Xolotl are what their authors built when they wanted more. Where no comparison exists For honesty's sake: I found no published figure for Sonar on any consumer two-card box; none for exo on NVIDIA hardware under Linux; no head-to-head between PolyStrata and Xolotl on any machine; no EXL3-versus-GGUF test in either direction; and no number for llama.cpp's RPC spread, only a report that it got slower. A benchmark page full of dashes is data too. How I verified this The figures above were gathered while compiling https://localai.hex7.com/benchmark.html, which marks each number with a source and states which machine it ran on. The sources collected there: Strata's README, its bench/results/2026-10-06-llamacpp-0.6.0 head-to-head and community-benchmarks files; PolyStrata's README, its 2026-10-11-laptop-qwen36-llamacpp-b11540 head-to-head and COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS file; Avalon's README tables (its runs against Strata v0.2.9 on the same boxes); Xolotl's README Gauntlet v3 table and speed log plus WILL_IT_RUN.md; the run table the ExLlama maintainers published for their earlier weights format; computingforgeeks' three-way test on rented cards; atomic.chat's Ollama-vs-llama.cpp on an RTX 5090; inventivehq's rows; developersdigest's write-up of llama.cpp PRs #29887 and #30112; Jeff Geerling's four-Mac-Studio exo test; dphnAI's Sonar measurement on four RTX PRO 6000; Spheron's measured vLLM H100 rows and its explicitly-modelled Aphrodite estimates; vLLM's own GB200/GB300 blog posts. This blog's engine notes record each project's own claims in detail. The one thing I could not verify is the machine at the centre of this article: two 16 GB cards with ~100 GB of RAM never ran in any published test. Mine will, and when it does I will publish those rows under the same rules as everyone else's.

articles.title: ExLlamaV3 and TabbyAPI - the pair that ships today, and what it asks of your hardware
articles.description: ExLlamaV3 and TabbyAPI are a pair documented by both projects: exllamav3's repository blurb reads "An optimized quantization and inference library for running LLMs locally on modern consumer-class GPUs", and tabbyAPI's reads "The official API server for Exllama. OAI compatible, lightweight, and fast." Everything below describes code that ships today; the hardware story changed with it, because ExLlamaV3 (turboderp-org/exllamav3, MIT, v1.6.6 of 31 October 2026) documents CPU offloading for mixture-of-experts weights, and TabbyAPI (theroyallab/tabbyAPI, AGPL-3.0) exposes it as a configuration knob - including on a machine like mine: two 16 GB consumer cards and ~100 GB of system RAM. What changed from ExLlamaV2 All verified in the repos themselves: The exllamav2 README carries a note at the top: "This project is archived for now. Development continues on ExLlamaV3." The V2 line is where EXL2 files lived; it is frozen. TabbyAPI removed its ExLlamaV2 backend on 14 July 2026 in a commit titled "Backends: Remove ExLlamaV2 backend and container abstraction layer". The current tree lists only backends/exllamav3 plus an embeddings backend; the sample config's backend comment reads "Options: exllamav3". Supported model types are now listed as "Exl3 (Highly recommended)" and FP16/BF16. EXL3 itself - quantisation "based on QTIP" - exists only in ExLlamaV3; the exllamav2 README and bundled docs never mention it. Neither project documents that ExLlamaV3 loads older EXL2 files - third-party posts claim it does - so treat migration as a model-file decision you cannot assume away. What it is The engine The engine README lists the feature set plainly: EXL3 quantisation based on QTIP plus "2-8 bit cache quantization", "Flexible tensor-parallel and expert-parallel inference for consumer hardware setups", and - the new one - "CPU offloading - Allows large MoE models to run with limited GPU resources. AVX2 and AVX512 support." The library compiles a Torch C++ extension; prebuilt wheels must match platform, Python, CUDA and PyTorch versions, while the PyPI build compiles from source and needs the CUDA toolkit installed. EXL3 is "a streamlined variant of QTIP from Cornell RelaxML": conversion takes an HF-format model plus a target bitrate and runs in one step - "a couple of minutes for smaller models, up to a few hours for larger ones (70B+)" on one high-end consumer card. Fractional bitrates are documented: the conversion guide's examples write directories like llama3.1-70b-instruct-exl3-3.75bpw, and an -hq flag promotes attention-class layers, the docs candid about a "(0.05 - 0.10 bpw)" size increase for a disproportionately large fidelity gain. The README maintains an architecture-support table (including DeepSeek V3/V4, some multimodal) rather than making per-model claims. The API layer TabbyAPI is "A FastAPI based application" that today serves text through the ExLlamaV3 backend; it also calls itself "the official API backend server for ExllamaV3". Features: tool/function calling, JSON schema, regex and EBNF grammars, Jinja2 chat templates, speculative decoding via draft models, continuous batching with paged attention ("for Nvidia Ampere GPUs and higher"), HF model downloading and embeddings. The sample config defaults the server to port 5000. GitHub's tags and releases API returns nothing for this repository; pyproject.toml carries version 0.0.1; installation is from the repo via pip install -U .[cu12] and friends, with CUDA Docker images (including a ROCm tag for Radeon RX 7900-series cards). The README's disclaimer says plainly: "TabbyAPI is a hobby project made for a small amount of users. It is not meant to run on production servers." How the pair works The chain starts with convert.py: an HF checkpoint plus a target bitrate becomes EXL3 safetensors - that is where quantised files on Hugging Face come from. The engine then exposes documented primitives: tensor/expert parallelism across GPUs, continuous dynamic batching, speculative decoding, 2-8 bit cache quantisation. TabbyAPI turns these into OpenAI-style endpoints governed by config.yml - which is also where the hardware switches live (next section). The pairing is stated in both directions: ExLlamaV3's README says "Looking for a server? TabbyAPI is the official and recommended backend server", and TabbyAPI's README/FAQ answers "What does TabbyAPI run?" with ExLlamaV3. Today that is the only documented combination. What it asks of your hardware The default placement is still weights-on-card. TabbyAPI's config documents gpu_split ("Array of VRAM sizes to split between GPUs, in GB"), an autosplit reserve of ~96 MB per GPU for loading, and tensor parallelism with a backend choice - "Native is recommended for PCIe GPUs, NCCL is recommended for NVLink". Its Docker notes add a hard requirement: "ExLlamaV3 uses POSIX shared memory for tensor parallelism and CPU MoE offload", with the default 64 MiB /dev/shm called out as too small. What changed, and what matters for a 2×16 GB + ~100 GB RAM machine, is the MoE offload path. It is documented twice - in ExLlamaV3's doc/env_vars.md and in TabbyAPI's server options: The engine flag is "Experimental: -mcl/--moe_cpu_offload … run the routed experts of the first N block-sparse MoE layers on the CPU, expert weights resident in system RAM, freeing the VRAM those layers' experts would have used." It names constraints: layer-split mode only (not tensor parallelism), mul1-codebook experts, K ≤ 8, uniform per-expert biases; "ineligible layers fall back to the GPU as usual". A worker process per model component owns its expert weights and a job ring in pinned shared memory, and during prefill "hot experts additionally stream their weights to the GPU and run there … while the CPU works the remaining tail". TabbyAPI exposes two variants: cpu_moe_offload_layers (whole layers on CPU) and cpu_moe_split_experts, which "splits every MoE layer instead of offloading whole layers, overlapping CPU and GPU compute, with dynamic placement keeping hot experts in VRAM". A pinned-arena option keeps expert weights page-locked; its own comment states the cost: "about 0.2 s per GiB of offloaded experts at load". The docs carry numbers, with their own disclaimer ("These are workload-specific measurements"): fully-offloaded mistral-small-4 119B with 54 GiB of experts went from 700 to 1850 tokens/s prefill on a PCIe gen5 x16 link using the pinned arena, "decode unchanged within noise"; and about 240 tok/s decode for LFM2.5-8B on a Threadripper 7960X with tuned thread counts (versus 222-232 in default configuration). Both are one-machine measurements quoted by the project, not guarantees. For my rig specifically: the sources do establish a documented mechanism for running large MoE models with experts partly or wholly out of system RAM, on consumer cards, placed via layer split rather than tensor parallelism - two 16 GB cards splitting weights by gpu_split plus ~100 GB of RAM for expert weights is within what that mechanism is built for. They establish no sizing numbers: neither project states VRAM/RAM minimums or worked examples on 16 GB-class cards ("not stated"). The measured 54 GiB of experts above would fit inside my ~100 GB budget, but whether a specific model fits is arithmetic I would invent if I quoted it as fact. Constraints to note: this is MoE-only ("Only affects MoE models"), dense models still have to fit in combined VRAM, and the path is marked experimental. The >=80-100 tok/s versus GGUF-CPU-offloading figure circulating for this stack remains unverified: no project source states it or compares itself to llama.cpp at all. Third-party comparisons exist (atomic.chat's EXL3-vs-GGUF benchmark; a dev.to run of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with the experts on CPU under 40 GB of RAM) - links below, labelled as community figures I have not reproduced. Where it fits / where it does not Fits: a single-user self-hosted OpenAI-compatible API on consumer NVIDIA hardware (Ampere or newer for parallel batching; ROCm images target Radeon RX 7900-series), with quantisation under your control, and a documented route to large MoE models on modest cards - the CPU-expert knobs, experimental as they are marked, are exactly what a 2×16 GB + 100 GB machine wants. Does not fit: production traffic (TabbyAPI's own disclaimer); dense models larger than combined VRAM (the offload path affects "MoE models" only); the V2-era EXL2 estate - that line is archived, and I could not confirm current engines read its files. The pair publishes no sizing chart: whether a specific model fits your machine is yours to measure. How I verified this Primary sources fetched on 11 November 2026: ExLlamaV3 README (master): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/master/README.md ; docs: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/master/doc/env_vars.md , https://raw.githubusercontent.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/master/doc/convert.md ExLlamaV3 metadata, licence (MIT), release v1.6.6 (31 Oct 2026) via the GitHub API TabbyAPI README: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/theroyallab/tabbyAPI/main/README.md ; config sample: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/theroyallab/tabbyAPI/main/config_sample.yml ; docs 01/02/05 via https://github.com/theroyallab/tabbyAPI/tree/main/docs ; LICENSE (AGPL-3.0); pyproject.toml (version 0.0.1; tags/releases absent via API) ExLlamaV2 backend removal commit: /commits?path=backends/exllamav2/model.py in the TabbyAPI commits API "Archived for now" note: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/turboderp/exllamav2/master/README.md llama.cpp README (for the offload counterpoint): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/master/README.md Community comparisons and claims found via search, not reproduced by me and not project sources: https://atomic.chat/blog/guides/exl3-vs-gguf , https://bestllmfor.com/guides/tabbyapi-self-hosted-openai-api/ (the latter asserts ExLlamaV3 can load EXL2 files) , https://dev.to/seppegadeyne/run-qwen38-flash-next-locally-with-exl3-and-tabbyapi-on-40-gb-of-ram-3m8d . Not established by any project source: the >=80-100 tok/s GGUF comparison; sizing numbers for 16 GB cards or ~100 GB machines; whether ExLlamaV3 reads EXL2 checkpoints; model counts on Hugging Face.

articles.title: Aphrodite Engine - a serving engine in the vLLM lineage, now renamed Sonar, and what my two 16 GB cards would need from it
articles.description: First, the finding that changes how this post should be read, because I checked it first: the repository at PygmalionAI/aphrodite-engine no longer exists under that name. The GitHub API returns a permanent redirect for it (repository id 657414607 - the same id behind dphnAI/sonar, created 23 June 2023); the README at main now describes the project as Sonar, and the one at tag v0.22.0 reads "Sonar (formerly Aphrodite Engine)". This is not a successor project that claims to continue it: it is the same repository, renamed in place. The commit that did it - "feat!: rename Aphrodite Engine to Sonar", dated 7 November 2026 - landed in v0.25.0, released 8 November 2026, the first release whose wheels are named sonar-*.whl. Until v0.24.1 (September 2026) they were aphrodite_engine-*.whl. What it is The current README describes Sonar as "an inference engine for Hugging Face-compatible language and multimodal models" providing "continuous batching, paged KV-cache management, optimized kernels, quantization, speculative decoding, and distributed serving". On lineage it states: "Sonar is based on vLLM. It includes additional model and quantization formats, sampling methods, kernels, platforms, and deployment features." It says the engine "serves production workloads for the Dolphin Inference Network and PygmalionAI" (now under the dphnAI org, with PygmalionAI still listed as a served deployment). The Aphrodite-era README, readable at old tags such as v0.10.0, used the same self-description: "Aphrodite is an inference engine that optimizes the serving of HuggingFace-compatible models at scale. Built on vLLM's Paged Attention technology, it delivers high-performance model inference for multiple concurrent users." It also states Aphrodite was "Developed through a collaboration between PygmalionAI and Ruliad", serving both organisations' chat platforms - so the project started, in its own words, as roleplay infrastructure. One v0.6.7-era README has a caution box worth quoting: "This project is not, and will never be, associated with any cryptocurrencies. Please do not fall for scams." Is it maintained? The GitHub API reports pushed_at 9 November 2026; the latest open release is v0.25.0 (8 November 2026). The licence is AGPL-3.0, per the LICENSE file at the repository root. The migration notice, as the project states it The Sonar docs have a "Migrate from Aphrodite" section: install sonar in a fresh virtual environment, because "the old aphrodite-engine PyPI package does not install the renamed release". Imports and CLI change from aphrodite to sonar, environment variables from APHRODITE_* to SONAR_* with no fallback, identifiers like AphroditeConfig become SonarConfig. The temporary aphrodite command "forwards to Sonar and warns at startup"; native wheels and serialized objects from the two eras "are not interchangeable". How it works The core is vLLM's: continuous batching and paged KV-cache management, as both eras of the README say. What keeps the lineage claim precise is the commit history: merge commits titled "chore(sync): sync to upstream " and "port vLLM through ", plus "[sync]" commits annotated "Upstream-vLLM: ". This is a downstream fork of vLLM that periodically pulls from upstream - stated by its own release notes, not inferred. What it adds, in the README's key-features list: prefix caching enabled by default; tensor, pipeline, data and expert parallelism; "Multi-node multiprocessing without a Ray cluster"; prefill/decode disaggregation through NIXL and other KV connectors; quantized weights and FP8 KV cache; speculative decoding with MTP, EAGLE, DSpark, DFlash and n-gram methods; structured output, reasoning parsers and automatic tool calling; image, audio and video models; LoRA serving; Prometheus metrics; and a set of front-end APIs - OpenAI, Anthropic, pooling, scoring, reranking, transcription and Kobold. The quantization reference is what makes the support claims checkable: a matrix generated from the current source tree lists awq, auto_awq, gptq, gptq_marlin, awq_marlin, FP8 variants, exl3, bitsandbytes, compressed-tensors, the ModelOpt family, mxfp4, torchao and more, each with a minimum NVIDIA streaming-multiprocessor capability; the page notes "NVIDIA CUDA accepts all registered methods". The v0.10.0 README listed AQLM, AutoRound, AWQ, BitNet, Bitsandbytes, EETQ, GGUF, GPTQ, QuIP#, SqueezeLLM, Marlin, FP2-FP12 and others in its feature bullet. One caution about the older ExLlama format: the current matrix lists exl3, not EXL2, and while every old README I saw credits Exllamav2 in acknowledgements, no feature list names EXL2 as a method - so the project does not state EXL2 support anywhere I looked. The samplers it has claimed since 2024 (DRY, XTC, Mirostat) and the Kobold API stay roleplay-facing: both eras of the README put the server on port 2242, and the old README pointed at SillyTavern. What it asks of your hardware The README's requirements at v0.22.0: Linux or Windows via WSL2; Python 3.10 to 3.13; CUDA 12 or newer. The current installer covers Linux x86-64 with NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm or CPU, Arm64, and Apple-silicon macOS with Metal; the full installation guide adds Intel XPU, Google TPU and Docker paths. On VRAM the README is explicit: "By design, Sonar takes up 92% of your GPU's VRAM", pointing at --gpu-memory-utilization if that is unwanted. For multiple cards, the parallelism page gives the design in order: "Start with one GPU. Add parallelism only when one GPU cannot meet the memory or throughput requirement." Tensor parallelism splits each layer across GPUs and should stay "within one NVLink or high-bandwidth GPU domain"; pipeline parallelism communicates less often and can cross nodes; data parallelism makes replicas; expert parallelism moves only MoE layers. The failure-pattern table lists "More GPUs reduce throughput" - cause: "Communication dominates". For my own rig - two 16 GB consumer cards, about 100 GB of system RAM - everything here is framed as what that machine would need from the engine, because I ran nothing and quote no numbers. From Sonar I would need a model that fits, once quantised, in both cards' combined VRAM - and the matrix's per-method GPU-generation notes are where I'd check whether my cards are even permitted for the format I choose. A two-card tensor-parallel group over plain PCIe sits exactly where the docs advise care: consumer boards have no NVLink domain. The ~100 GB of system RAM buys me nothing on the pages I checked: the model-storage page covers Hugging Face caches, offline snapshots and load formats - no weight tiering into system RAM anywhere. Where it fits / where it does not This blog's other engine notes - llama.cpp, Strata, Avalon, PolyStrata and Xolotl - all bet that weights belong in system RAM or on NVMe and move through the bus as needed: Xolotl's README describes itself as "Built from Strata, and grown a long way past it" carrying MoE experts up from RAM and drives; Avalon's runs its model with "the experts in system RAM" on one consumer card. Sonar/Aphrodite is the opposite bet, and its own README states the lineage: weights sit on GPUs, split across ranks when they must, and the engine's job is throughput for many concurrent users rather than making a too-big model fit anyway. On my two cards that means Sonar is only the right shape if a quantised model fits in both together; for the flagship-class MoEs that family chases, nothing in the pages I fetched competes with Xolotl's expert tiering. Where else it does not fit: the licence is AGPL-3.0, which rules it out for stacks that cannot ship AGPL code. And name-hygiene matters now - the old Pygmalion docs host, aphrodite.pygmalion.chat, serves a certificate that does not match its hostname and returned nothing usable when I checked; anything current is at sonar.dphn.ai and github.com/dphnAI/sonar; the migration page above covers upgrades under the new name. How I verified this All fetched on 11 November 2026: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PygmalionAI/aphrodite-engine/main/README.md - current README: Sonar self-description, key features, install, APIs; served from dphnAI/sonar via redirect. https://api.github.com/repos/PygmalionAI/aphrodite-engine - HTTP 301 to https://api.github.com/repositories/657414607, returning dphnAI/sonar: "Large-scale LLM inference engine", created 2023-06-23, pushed 2026-11-09, AGPL-3.0. https://api.github.com/repos/dphnAI/sonar/releases and /releases/tags/v0.25.0 - release list and notes (wheel renaming, sync and rename commits). https://api.github.com/repos/dphnAI/sonar/commits/49c386154f51369bfaf563d8ed9768dbf5269d71 - rename commit, 2026-11-07. READMEs at tags v0.24.1, v0.22.0, v0.10.0, v0.6.7 via https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dphnAI/sonar//README.md - old self-descriptions, feature lists, requirements, 92%-VRAM note; tag listing via https://api.github.com/repos/dphnAI/sonar/tags. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dphnAI/sonar/main/LICENSE - AGPL-3.0. https://sonar.dphn.ai/reference/quantization/, /getting-started/upgrading/, /deployment/parallelism/, /deployment/model-storage/ and https://aphrodite.pygmalion.chat (certificate mismatch; nothing usable) - quant matrix, migration notice, parallelism guidance, model-loading scope. Comparison family: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Indras-Mirror/Xolotl/main/README.md (built on Strata), https://raw.githubusercontent.com/freriadoc/Avalon/main/README.md (llama.cpp fork, experts in RAM), https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Niko1221/Strata/main/README.md ("Run powerful AI on your own computer"). My earlier notes: posts/xolotl-blog.md, posts/polystrata-blog.md, posts/avalon-wordpress.md.

articles.title: exo - splitting one model across several machines, and the rules it sets for joining
articles.description: I went looking at exo (github.com/exo-explore/exo) because it answers the question I keep getting about a constrained rig: what if the memory ceiling of one machine were not the ceiling? The repository's own description reads, plainly enough: "Run frontier AI locally" - and the README states what it does in one sentence: "exo connects all your devices into an AI cluster." Not just larger models, but, with day-0 support for RDMA over Thunderbolt 5, faster as you add machines. The GitHub metadata as I fetched it on 11 November 2026: 48,311 stars, Apache-2.0, Python, created in June 2024, last pushed on 6 November 2026 - maintained by exo labs, and active. What it is exo is a peer-to-peer cluster runtime: you run the same software on each machine - a desktop, a laptop, a second box over Wi-Fi or Ethernet - and it forms a cluster without manual configuration. Devices discover each other automatically, provided they are on the same network and run the same version of exo; devices on different versions simply do not join each other. Each node serves its own API and dashboard at http://localhost:52415. The inference backend is MLX, Apple's framework, with MLX distributed for cluster communication. Models come from HuggingFace (search and "add a custom model" endpoints are built in; models needing trust_remote_code require an explicit opt-in). There is an offline mode (EXO_OFFLINE=true), read-only model directories for shared storage such as NFS mounts, and four API surfaces: OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, Claude Messages and Ollama. The docs: existing clients - OpenWebUI included - just point their base URL at exo. One honest note: exo-labs.github.io/exo returns a GitHub Pages 404 today, so I verified nothing from it; this piece relies on the repository. How it works Discovery, and the rules for joining The version rule is stricter than it sounds. Devices join only when they share a cluster name (a namespace flag), a "wire version" - a number exo bumps whenever what devices send each other changes - and a build. The macOS app numbers itself with its own release number while source checkouts keep their package version, so an app and a source build on one network do not join each other by default. A Mac and a Linux machine do not join at all, even on the same commit, because they run different builds of MLX. Guest Wi-Fi and some office networks block discovery outright; when a device is seen but cannot join, the dashboard says "DEVICE ON ANOTHER EXO VERSION". There is also a role knob: --no-worker runs a node that coordinates networking and orchestration but executes no inference, which the README recommends for machines without GPU resources but with good connectivity. Placement: topology-aware, before the first token The README calls this "Topology-Aware Auto Parallel": exo picks how to split a model from a realtime view of the device topology, taking device resources and per-link latency and bandwidth into account. You can watch the machinery from the API: GET /instance/previews returns every valid placement for a model, with a memory delta per node, before you commit to one. Launching is asynchronous; you wait for readiness on an SSE endpoint. The README claims tensor-parallel sharding reaches "up to 1.8x speedup on 2 devices and 3.2x speedup on 4 devices" - the project's own figures, not independent benchmarks. The bundled exo-bench tool measures prefill and generation speeds across placement configurations, treating "ring" and "jaccl" instance types and pipeline versus tensor sharding as things you choose between. RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 RDMA is a macOS 26.2 capability; the README claims a "99% reduction in latency between devices". It requires Macs with Thunderbolt 5, TB5 cables, every machine cabled to every other one, matching OS versions down to beta numbers, and a recovery-mode rdma_ctl enable. The benchmark set linked from the README was run by Jeff Geerling (18 December 2025): four M3 Ultra Mac Studios with 1.5 TB of combined unified memory at ~$40,000. He notes that RDMA cuts memory-access latency from about 300 microseconds to under 50 (citing an MLX pull request); found llama.cpp's RPC method losing speed as nodes were added while exo gained; and got about 32 tokens/s on Qwen3-235B (8-bit) and "around 30" on Kimi K2 Thinking on the full cluster. He also reported stability problems with the then-prerelease software, and rebooted the cluster a lot. What happens when a device leaves The API reference (docs/api.md) treats a dropped machine as a first-class error: an in-flight generation ends with a device_left code - or out_of_memory, gpu_timeout, model_stalled - rather than a hung request, and a launch is refused if the devices turn out not to have the memory for it. That is behaviour worth knowing about before you put an agent on it. What it asks of your hardware The macOS app needs Apple silicon and macOS Sequoia 15.1 or later; RDMA needs macOS Tahoe 26.2 and a Thunderbolt 5 Mac (the README lists the M4 Pro Mac mini, M4 Max Mac Studio, M4 Max MacBook Pro and M3 Ultra Mac Studio). From source, macOS wants Xcode, uv, Node, Rust; Linux wants the same toolchain but the README is blunt: "Currently, exo runs on CPU on Linux. GPU support for Linux platforms is under development." It asks users to open or upvote feature requests for hardware they want supported. Every device must run the same version of exo, be reachable on the same network, and download or hold the model. Mixed clusters in the consumer sense - a Mac and an NVIDIA Linux box in one group - do not join today. For my own rig - two 16 GB consumer GPUs and about 100 GB of system RAM - what this machine would need from exo, on the README's current terms: CPU inference on Linux (the MLX backend does not use those cards on Linux yet), a model split across shared system memory, and no RDMA path. The project does not state a supported layout for that machine, and I ran nothing, so I am quoting no numbers for it. Where it fits / where it does not Where it fits: a homogeneous all-Apple-silicon fleet with Thunderbolt 5 between them, where you genuinely want frontier-class models - the README's own showcase is DeepSeek v3.1 671B (8-bit) and Kimi K2 Thinking on four Mac Studios - and where a drop-in OpenAI-, Claude- or Ollama-compatible endpoint is the integration point you care about. The placement preview API and exo-bench are the tools for deciding how many machines a given model needs before you buy them. Where it does not fit: my family stack, which I have covered here in detail - Strata, PolyStrata, Avalon and Xolotl, which tiers MoE experts across VRAM, system RAM and NVMe. Those projects attack the same ceiling from inside one machine: keep the fast silicon you have, move weights through a memory hierarchy you control. llama.cpp's RPC path, per Geerling's write-up, spreads layers across nodes but loses performance as nodes are added - the exact failure mode exo's tensor-parallel-over-RDMA design is built to avoid. exo does something different in kind: it grows the memory pool across machines and plans from a topology view. What it does not do is any expert-tiering equivalent - there is no such mechanism in its README or API docs, and the project does not claim one. On a consumer-NVIDIA rig it is simply not yet a target: Linux is CPU-only, and Mac nodes refuse to join Linux nodes. If your fleet is Macs, that is fine; if it is this lab, exo today is an interesting read, not a deployment. How I verified this Sources fetched on 11 November 2026: README (primary): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/exo-explore/exo/main/README.md - features, version rules, RDMA requirements, Linux CPU-only statement, benchmark captions. GitHub API for the repo: https://api.github.com/repos/exo-explore/exo - stars, licence, creation and push dates. Docs folder listing: https://api.github.com/repos/exo-explore/exo/contents/docs (contains api.md) and https://api.github.com/repos/exo-explore/exo/contents/.github (workflows, CODEOWNERS). API reference: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/exo-explore/exo/main/docs/api.md - placement, await, error codes. Project site https://exo-labs.github.io/exo - returned a GitHub Pages 404 on the day I checked; nothing verified from it. Benchmark article linked by the README: https://www.jeffgeerling.com/blog/2025/15-tb-vram-on-mac-studio-rdma-over-thunderbolt-5 - Geerling's figures, caveats and llama.cpp comparison, dated 18 December 2025.

articles.title: A Google News alert with the real article URLs (not news.google.com redirects)
articles.description: Google News RSS is the easiest way to monitor a brand, a competitor or a topic in any country — until you notice that every link is a news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMi… redirect. You can't dedupe by publisher URL, you can't fetch the article, and your Slack alerts look like spam. Google News Scraper with Original Article URLs (disclosure: I built it) resolves those links to the publisher's real URL and returns headline, publisher, date and snippet for any query, language and country. from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN") run = client.actor("fujiwaranosai/google-news-scraper").call(run_input={ "queries": ['"Anthropic" OR "OpenAI"', "Tesla -recall"], "timeRange": "1d", "language": "en", "country": "us", "onlyNew": True, }) for a in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items(): print(a["published_at"], a["publisher"], a["title"], a["article_url"]) Ideas PR monitoring: one query per brand/executive, schedule hourly with timeRange: "1h" and onlyNew. Market research: track tickers or sectors per country edition (es/mx, pt/br, de/de). AI digests: pass article_url to your content crawler and summarize the day's news with an LLM. Google News operators work too: "exact phrase", OR, -exclude, site:reuters.com. The first 100 articles of every account are free. More ready-to-run examples: https://github.com/novosai0day-a11y/public-data-apis

articles.title: How I Started Writing on DEV.to, and You Can Too
articles.description: Hello, New DEV.to members!to Members! I am Tyler N, a 13-year-old (almost 14) from Maryland, and I made my first article here on DEV.to, or on any sort of blogging platform, on May 28, 2026, which was 167 days, 24 weeks, or 5 months ago. It was titled "Git for GitHub: How to use simple Git commands to manage a GitHub repository," and it definitely took me a while to write. But after I published it, I realized that I would be making many more articles here on DEV.to. I had received real comments on it about how it actually, really helped people. I thought it wouldn't go anywhere, but it definitely did. I started to learn to code sometime in the sixth grade (which was in the 2024-2025 school year), created my first GitHub repository in December of 2025, and DEV.to is just the natural continuation of that. Since that point, I have made six more articles. My second article was about how I used Inkscape to create a banner for the first article and my profile picture. While it may definitely be a brisk pace, I had sleepaway camp and summer right in the middle, so it just about evens it out. While making these articles, I have gotten much better at my writing, both technical and non-technical. The point of me telling you this is to inform you that you can absolutely do the same thing I did, if not better than me. To find the idea for that very first article, and just about every article after it, I thought about either something that was confusing for me or that I thought might be confusing to others, or a coding project I had recently gotten to a stable state. I also wrote one about why I chose to code in the Terminal, without an Integrated Development Environment (IDE). Obviously, these aren't the only things articles can be about. Be creative, and start writing! If you don't think you can write an article just yet, go around and explore other people's articles, and interact with them by leaving thoughtful comments. How did you guys discover DEV.to, and what are you going to write? Feel free to describe how you got into coding or another technical field.

articles.description: Nats chief says he ‘quite enjoyed’ ignoring calls from Ryanair CEO to quit over system outages in September Business live – latest updates The boss of Nats has said he was “the most disliked person in the UK” after air traffic control systems failed twice in September, disrupting flights for hundreds of thousands of passengers. He told an aviation industry conference: “My name is Martin Rolfe, I’m the CEO of Nats – or as I like to think of myself, the most disliked person in the UK in September.” Continue reading...
